entities.summary:
Osaka is the third-largest city in Japan and the largest city in the Kansai (Kinki) region of western Honshū, with a population of 2.7 million in the city proper and 19 million in the greater metropolitan area. Known historically as the 'kitchen of Japan' (Tenka no Daidokoro) for its role as the nation's commercial and food distribution center, Osaka has a distinctively irreverent, mercantile culture — captured in the local saying 'Kyoto people ruin themselves through over-dressing; Osaka people through over-eating.'

Osaka Castle, built by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in 1583, made the city Japan's political center during the late Warring States period. The Siege of Osaka (1614–1615), in which Tokugawa Ieyasu destroyed the castle and killed Hideyori Toyotomi, completed the Tokugawa unification of Japan and marked the beginning of the Edo period (1603–1868). Under Tokugawa rule, Osaka became Japan's primary commercial city — home to the rice brokers, money exchangers, and commodity markets that financed the feudal system. Osaka Dojima Rice Exchange (1697) was one of the world's first commodity futures markets.

Modern Osaka was Japan's industrial heartland in the Meiji and Taisho eras. It suffered severe bombing in World War II and was rebuilt as a manufacturing and commercial hub. Osaka hosted the 1970 World Expo (the most visited Expo in history at 64 million visitors) and is scheduled to host Expo 2025. Universal Studios Japan and the proposed integrated resort casino (if approved) represent its 21st-century tourism ambitions.
